speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to
move the motion of which I gave notice yesterday:
That on and after Monday, 8th April next, and all subsequent Mondays and Wednesdays till the end of the session, government notices of motion and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except questions and notices of motions for the production of papers.

Mr. Speaker, I think this motion requires a little consideration. I am entirely in accord with it as regards Wednesdays, but it seems to me that the government should not appropriate Mondays at this stage of the session to the exclusion of private bills. Yesterday the Prime Minister stated that up to the present private members have had eleven days this session to discuss their motions. This is true, but as a matter of fact so far private bills have occupied practically no time of the house whatever. According to the rules the first item on Mondays is private bills. I find that so far on Mondays private bills have occupied only one column in Hansard, and that was on February 25. In other words, at the beginning of the session private bills are referred to committees, and there discussed; they do not take up much time in the house, but later on in the session very often they require to be discussed on the floor. At the end of last session several very important private bills were left stranded on the order paper. Manifestly this is unfair to the petitioners, and I think it is not consistent with the dignity of the house that these bills should not be dealt with during the session. The procedure governing petitions for private bills is set forth in great detail in the book of rules. If the rules are complied with by the petitioners, and the bills are introduced for consideration at a reasonably early stage in the session, 78594-621
it matters not whether the petitioners be public companies or private individuals, I submit that they should be dealt with, whatever the decision thereon may be.
Last session the Prime Minister introduced a motion similar to this. I find that after it was agreed to there were seven Mondays that the house sat when private bills could not be taken up. I believe that if the house had not agreed to the Prime Minister's motion the difficulties that confronted us towards the end of the session would have been avoided, and those private bills would not have been left to the tender mercies of Tuesday and Friday evenings, which resulted in some of them not being disposed of at prorogation.
If my memory serves me right, Mr. Speaker, when I first entered the house the custom was for the government to take Wednesdays fairly early in the session, but they did not appropriate Mondays until the session was well advanced. I quite realize that this motion is drafted in exactly the same terms as the one which the Prime Minister moved last session, and I have been wondering why that wording is used. I have come to the conclusion that the form is similar to that which was used when Wednesdays only were taken over for government business. As I say, I do not remember that it was the practice for the government to give their business precedence over private bills on Mondays until towards the end of the session. To my mind this change in the old practice has produced what may be called not a proper state of affairs so far as private bills are concerned.
If private bills are allowed first place on the order paper for Mondays, I submit to the Prime Minister that the work of the session would not be delayed at all. After the private bills had been disposed of on Mondays the government would have the rest of tlhe day for their legislation following questions and notices of motion for production of papers. But if there are private bills on the order paper, then I submit that they should have consideration in the first place on Mondays, as provided in the rules. If the Prime Minister will consider for a moment, I think he will agree with me that the effect of this present motion would be practically to deprive private bills of their right to the first place on Mondays throughout the session, and in that case he might as well make a motion for changing the rules altogether; because up to this time private bills have taken only one column of Hansard on a Monday. Of course, when I say this. I have not in mind any particular private bill; it is immaterial whether they be divorce
Private Members' Days

bills or private bills of any other character, or bills in respect to companies. Private bills, in my opinion, should be proceeded with on Mondays according to the rule. I realize that the Prime Minister and the government are responsible for the conduct of the business of the house, and I have no idea of moving any amendment to the motion, but I submit to the Prime Minister that it would be better to adhere to the practice that obtained in the old days, so that private bills would hold their place on Mondays. Otherwise, I am willing that the motion should carry, so that government business would come next after questions and notices of motions for the production of papers on both Mondays and Wednesdays.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the electors of the constituency of Skeena, who honoured me by sending me to this house to represent their views, placed upon me two duties, first that I shall take an interest in all that appertains to Canada with regard to her internal and external affairs and secondly that I might represent them and place their views and their needs before this honourable house. Otherwise I would not presume to say anything in this debate after the wonderful address delivered by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie); his was a masterpiece of reasoning which as yet has not been contradicted in any important detail by any of the hon. members who have spoken since.
Before I introduce the subject upon which I would like to speak to-day I would state briefly that the budget is already before the people of Canada; its merits and demerits are known to everyone. The working men of Canada have read it with interest; the agriculturists, the fishermen on our coasts, the lonely lighthouse keepers who keep watch and ward over the carriers of our commerce -the ships that pass in the night-all have read the budget. Likewise the hard-working and poorly-paid lower classes of the civil servants of this country have read it; but the millions of people who are not stockholders in large corporations, who are not presidents of banks, who do not pay income tax or drive the high-powered motor cars referred to yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), do not find very much meat or comfort in the budget presented in this house on Friday, March 1. When I was considering the budget I thought it would have been a very good thing if the Minister of Finance had taken a leaf from the book of those wonderful, canny Scots who in 1670 created the Hudson's Bay Company, because it seems to me that in all our trade relations which I have had time to read the Minister of Finance or whoever has negotiated
The Budget-Mr. Brady

the arrangements has been given the thin end of the stick. In those days, Mr. Speaker, when the Hudson's Bay Company traded with the Indians, the measurement of value was skins piled to the height of a rifle, and the canny Scots of those days took jolly good care that the barrel of the rifle was longer than that of the ordinary rifle then in use.
Now, Mr. Speaker, coming to the chief points of my short address to-day, I think it will be a revelation to any thinking Canadian who analyses the trade figures of Canada to discover some cogent truths which I do not think can be contradicted either inside or outside of this house. I am going to make a statement now which has been thoughtfully considered, and before this budget debate is concluded I would like it answered. It is this: Canada to-day is finding it more difficult than ever to retain the major portion of the financial value and the nation-building value of her natural resources and products, in spite of the wealth of her great natural resources. Let me give some figures in connection with the great basic industry of mining, whose development has been a revelation to the world and the admiration of less fortunate nations. Is our mining industry to-day an asset or a liability to the people of this country? That is the question, and what is the answer? It is a terrible indictment against this government to be forced to say that the wealth of our mines, running into millions, is not an asset to Canada. Here is what we did in the nine months ending December 31, 1928: We sent to the United States $135,000,000 worth of semi-raw or semi-manufactured products from our three mineral groups, and we imported $437,000,000 worth. Those are the figures representing the trade in this great basic industry.
What does that mean? It means, in simple language that a child can understand, that for every day of those nine months Canada sent out of the country $1,000,000 to buy goods which could be manufactured in our own country. Shall I bring it a little nearer? For every hour of each day of the nine months we sent out of Canada $84,000 to buy goods which could be manufactured here. Shall I bring it still nearer? Every time the clock in the Victory Tower ticked off a minute we sent out $1,400.

speechtext: Cash?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, sir. If we had stopped there it might not be so bad, but together with that money we sent the very cream of the intellect of this young nation. Furthermore let me add that when the government [Mr. Brady.3
failed to respond to the needs of technical education in this country and refused the grant, they took a retrograde step from which they will not recover. We are losing from Canada our very brightest scientists and cleverest men. Here is an example; Professor Dickson, one of the brilliant research men of Macdonald college, was receiving a salary of only $3,500, and he was offered a position in Australia at a salary which Canada should have doubled if necessary to keep him here. He was offered a position in an Australian university at a salary of $7,500. And thus it goes on. It is not the fate of any political party which is at stake but the soul and life of Canada, and someone will have to answer for it before very long.
If we could take just half of the manufactured goods we import from the United States over $800,000,000, and manufacture them here and keep $400,000,000 in Canada to circulate here and build up our domestic industries, what could we do with it? We could solve the problem of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) over night. What a pitiable travesty it is on the days when Canada loomed as the bright star in the centre of this great empire, when we realize that the government of Canada could not reply to the questions asked in the House of Commons at London two days ago. A Labour member of that house asked, " Can the dominions do anything with their great natural wealth to give employment to our highly trained artisans and industrial workers who are out of work?" The one who replied to that question was the head of the Labour Federation in Canada, Mr. Tom Moore, and he said, "There is not a chance for them at all." There is no chance yet, but if our party comes into power I say that not only would every boy and young man in Canada be given a chance to live here, and earn his living but we could assist the motherland as well, and invite the best stock of Europe and give them all work. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when he was in London at the time of Queen Victoria's jubilee, in the course of a speech said, and I think his words have a present-day significance:
England has proved at all times that she can fight her own battles, but, if ever the day was to come when she was in danger, let the bugle sound, let the fires be lit on the hills and in all parts of the empire, and though we might not be able to do much, whatever we can do shall be done to help her.
Those are the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but the members on the other side of the house do not seem to like them.

It is too deep for them.

The Budget-Mr. Brady

speechtext:
the sons and daughters of Canada to be checked on all sides without being ahle to attain their natural heritage? The fishermen in Prince Rupert are not getting a square deal. The other day an hon. gentleman across the floor went so far as to say: "Do not retaliate." He used the wrong word; there is no retaliation at all; the question is one of protection of ourselves and of our industries.
I should like to refer to another matter which will disclose what is happening in Canada to-day. I took the trade figures for 1928 dealing with Canada and the United States, and1 I took the same for Canada and Great Britain for the same period. There was an adverse balance of trade between Canada and the United States, amounting to 1241,500,000, while with Great Britain we had a favourable balance of trade amounting to $224,800,000. Put in the plainest words imaginable, that money should have been kept within Canada and had that been the case there would have been no need for the minister to worry night after night how to increase the population of this great country; we would have the money to circulate within our own country. W'hat happened to the money we got from Great Britain? It went into the United States to pay for our adverse trade balance with them. That is the answer and there is no use in our endeavouring to fool ourselves. The fiscal policy of the present government is hopelessly wrong for Canada. The Minister of Finance said the other day: " If we have any fiscal problems." Why, the destiny of a country depends upon its fiscal policy 1	That fiscal
policy has a certain objective. If it fails in that, if the' theory that they enunciate does not become converted into concrete action of benefit to the people, it is a failure.
To sum up, let me say that with the spread of education throughout the whole country, things are not going unnoticed The man who wears overalls has as great and profound knowledge of life as he who sits in his Buick or sedan. The working people of Canada to-day are not in accord with what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) said. He said: "We are prosperous." Prosperity is a relative term and if we want real prosperity we must do something more for the masses than this government is doing. If we want to put Canada where she ought rightfully to be as the greatest dominion of the British Empire; if we want to increase Canada's population-

To those who anticipate the sentence I shall only say " Honi soit qui mal y pense." The biggest indictment upon this government is the fact that our population is standing still. It is all very well to talk about our wonderful external trade running into billions and about our wonderful plenipotentiaries in various capitals; but to compare ourselves to the United States population is to compare the little spaniel with the Newfoundland dog. The United States have a population of 117,000,000 whereas we have less than 10,000,000.
I feel this afternoon that what I have said is but a brief indication of what I would like to have referred to had I had more than forty minutes at my disposal. But in conclusion let me say that whatever the government may think or say, the soul of Canada has awakened and the rallying cry will be: " Canada for the Canadians and the great empire to which we belong.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I only wish, Mr. Speaker, that I was gifted with the eloquence of the member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) in presenting my case this afternoon.
I do not intend taking up very much time in discussing the budget, because I want to deal more particularly with the department over which I have the honour to preside, and as I have only forty minutes in which to speak at this time I intend to devote nearly all of my time to the question of immigration. Perhaps there is no subject that has been more discussed in the country than this same question. You can hardly pick up a newspaper to-day, or a periodical or a magazine, but you will find someone putting forth his views on immigration. The difficulty that I experience however is that there does not seem to be any unanimity in regard to this question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is your idea?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not yet heard from the member from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) any well defined policy on immigration. Labour looks askance at any large immigration into the country, afraid perhaps that it might increase unemployment and make it more difficult for the labouring classes. The railways, on the other hand, claim that the country could absorb a very much larger volume of immigration than is now coming into the country. And I am sure that the agriculturists are not pressing very hard for increased immigration at the present time. I have not

The Budge!-Mr. Forke
had much encouragement from that section of the public in regard to increasing the volume of immigration.
Notwithstanding the eloquent speech that we have just listened to from the hon. member for Skeena, conditions are not so very bad in Canada at the present time. It is the first time that I have heard the statement-and I hope it is not true-that the more wealth we take out of our mines the poorer we become. It seems a strange sort of argument and it is quite beyond me. Every sign points to the fact that things seem to be going fairly well with us. Commercial statistics, leading financial institutions, production, manufacturing, all point to growth and prosperity. The National railways which, a few years ago, were looked upon as a millstone around the peck of this young nation, are becoming, in fact, are a very valuable asset to the nation. Perhaps the only blot-if it can be called that-upon the situation at the present time, is the fact that our young people are not staying on the land but are moving into the cities in increasing numbers. That is not a very good thing for this Dominion, and that, Sir, I believe to be the greatest problem not only in Canada but the world over. It is not an uncommon thing for a Canadian family to leave a farm and to find a family from a foreign country coming in to take their place. While we speak about agriculture being one of our great problems, I do not agree with hon. members on the other side of the house who advocate a policy that would make it more difficult than it is at the present time. Judging from the speech we have just listened to, I am indeed surprised at the tepid amendment which has been offered to the budget by the opposition. I had expected an amendment that had some teeth in it, an amendment that would come out fairly and squarely and state what the trouble was.
A good deal of controversy exists in regard to continental and British immigration. I have never agreed, Mr. Speaker, that there are superior and inferior people. There are backward and forward people and backward and forward nations. We all know, looking into the dim past, that great nations have existed and have passed away, and left little more behind than a name. In more recent times, we also know that nations have reached the peak of progress and civilization and have then faded Out of the picture, as it were, and other nations have taken their place. That is what has happened in the past and doubtless the same will happen in the future. Some nationalities, however, are much more
easily absorbed than others, and we have to take that into consideration in considering this question of immigration.
I noticed an article in the Saskatoon Star the other day, from which I desire to quote. It states:
It is -unfortunate to have immigrants in the west without knowledge of English, with little, if any, money, with no experience of farm work as carried on in the west. Some of these people have been left stranded at country points without any immediate prospect of employment. It is not fair to leave men without funds, ignorant of English, to shift for themselves in a strange land-this is not colonization.
I quite agree with that sentiment, Mr. Speaker, and I trust, as Minister of Immigration, that I will do my best to prevent an occurrence of that kind. Such a thing as that is of no benefit to immigration. It is of no benefit to Canada to have people come here unable to find employment when they arrive.
Some statements have appeared in the public press lately, in regard to the railway agreement. I would like to say a few words in regard to that. As most of the hon. members know, the railway agreement was entered into to stimulate the supply of farm labour from certain named countries in Europe. I was in the west last summer, met representatives of the four provincial governments out there and discussed with them the supply of foreign farm labour. I had an estimate from the governments of the four western provinces as to what they considered would be required in their respective provinces. We also made an estimate in the department of the amount of labour required during the coming summer. I have only this to say, Sir, that the estimate made by the department was very much larger than that given to me by the various provinces. However, I came to the conclusion that thirty per cent of the single foreign farm labourers of last year's immigration would be sufficient to meet requirements for that class of labour in the three western provinces. There has been a good deal of criticism in regard to that regulation, but I am perfectly satisfied that there will be sufficient labour of that kind to meet all the requirements of the farmers in western Canada. There is no limit placed on families coming in to settle on the land from those countries, and there is no limit on relatives coming out under the regulations. There is no limit on domestics coming out from foreign countries, aud there is no quota. I have seen a resolution on the order paper that might be discussed, with regard to a quota; but there is no quota established in regard to that kind
The Budget-Mr. Forke

of immigration. And, Mr. Speaker, at the end of May, should it be found that there is a shortage of foreign labour, the doors can be opened. I feel it is my duty to see that people coming from countries, unable to speak our language, shall have employment when they do come. That is the only trouble that has arisen in regard to this matter.

I think that may be taken as a 'basic principle. Since 1881 five million immigrants have come into Canada. For the ten years from 1911 to 1921 1,728,921 immigrants came in. I am sorry the member for Skeena is not in his seat, for these figures would interest him in view of his remarks on immigration. Our net gain at the end of ten years was 491,281.

I do not wish to make any insinuations against the government then in power, but I want the house to pay particular attention to the fact that that exodus took place when no Liberal government was in office. So that the matter of trade policy or tariff-

I do not wish to draw any unwarranted inferences from those figures, but it is reasonable to state that perhaps the 166,782 immigrants that entered the Dominion for the calendar year 1928 and established

permanent homes here constitute a better record than for some of the preceding years when we had 400,000 immigrants annually. It is not the number of people who come in, it is the number who become permanent citizens of this Dominion that really count in immigration. It may be profitable to transportation and other agencies to have a large influx of immigrants who simply pass through the country to return no more, but this type of immigration is certainly not profitable nationally. Since 1881 our record for 1928 has been exceeded only seven times. In 1926, two years ago, 96,064 immigrants came in. Last year, as I have already mentioned, we received 166,782 immigrants.

speechtext: Where from?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will give their origin. British, 65,882, I would remind the house that the miner-harvesters are included in that total, and a few thousand should be deducted to cover those who returned to Great Britain. There were 29,900 from the United States, and 28,840 from northwestern Europe. This makes a total immigration from Great Britain, the United States and northwestern Europe of 114,622-all people very easily assimilated into our life. Southern and southeastern Europe sent 52,161, thus making the grand total of 166,782. Let me point out that 70,718 more immigrants came in during 1928 than two years ago.
Those who complain about our lack of immigration are fond of making comparisons with the United States, much to our disadvantage. Indeed, the hon. member for Skeena has just mentioned that we should take a leaf out of the United States' book in regard to immigration policy. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are getting a larger percentage of immigrants to our population than ever entered the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A higher percentage of immigrants to our population than ever entered the United States. When 840,000 immigrants came into the United States that country had a population of over one hundred million. With our population of nine and a half million, a total immigration for 1928 of 166,782 people gives a higher percentage in our favour. Consequently we have a bigger problem of assimilation and absorption than ever confronted the United States. That is something which should be borne in mind' by those who would like to pour millions and millions of immigrants into this country. Perhaps we have reached the point where we can about absorb the stream of immigrants now flowing in. As

The Budget-Mr. Forke
the country develops and capital increases there would be an increase in population, and under normal circumstances we shall be able to absorb more immigrants. In this connection I desire to quote a few lines from a speech delivered by Premier Baldwin when he visited Canada a few years ago. I should like to say that of all the distinguished visitors to this Dominion none have displayed such a grasp of the situation as Premier Baldwin and ex-Premier Lloyd George. They seemed to realize what we need in this young country. Speaking of immigration to Canada, Premier Baldwin said:
If it be no impertinence on my part to say one word to Canadians, I would say: The future is with you; do not be in too much of a hurry. Your country is a country for men from the north, the hardy, virile races. Quality before quantity any day. Build up with the best. What does it matter if it is a hundred years, or two hundred years, or more, before your country is full? Keep the stock you have, and the men and women you have, and see that the coming generations are in no way inferior to them. I have often thought that it is as dangerous a thing to the morals of a nation to get rich too quickly as it is to an individual. Time is on your side. Maintain the values. Maintain the standards. And may the prayer of Canada always be the prayer of the Greek sailor which has been preserved for us by Seneca: "0 God, You may save me if You will; You may sink me if You will; but, whatever happens, I will always keep my rudder true."
I think we may take that to heart as a good lesson in regard to our immigration problem.
During the past year there has been a large increase in the number of homesteads taken up. In the four western provinces during 1928 there were 15.566 homesteads taken up, compared with 6.356 in 1927-a gain of 250 per cent. In the Grande Prairie and Peace RiveT country 5,216 homesteads were taken up-a gain of 450 per cent over the previous year. Taking 160 acres as the unit for a homestead, it means that two and a half million acres of land vras homesteaded-not very bad progress when we are supposed to be standing still. The people represented by these homestead entries number 41,724. A great many of those homesteaders are young men from our own western prairies, and I hope some from the eastern part of the Dominion also. We can get no better type of colonization than that. The young fellows from our farms in western Canada go out to the new districts and there establish homes for themselves. They are the very best settlers, because, Mr. Speaker, there is no better settler than he who is born in some lone sheiling in Canada.
Last summer I had the pleasure of visiting the Grande PraJirie and Peace River country and was astonished to see the progress that had been made. I found fields of splendid wheat ripening in the sun in the month of Augffet, ten days earlier than the crop much further south-ten days earlier than around Edmonton, for instance. I do not think much of that wheat was damaged by early frost, whereas a great deal of such damage was done in Saskatchewan. It is a wonderful country, there is no doubt of it, and it will be rapidly developed in the not very distant future. But I would suggest that no one should get it into his mind that there are vast prairies in the Peace River district similar to those that were to be found in the western provinces away back in the nineties. The soil is good but it will take more labour and more capital to build up homes there than it did in the older districts. I had the privilege of attending a picnic at Peace River lodge, and about the best thing I saw, in Peace River was the people there. They reminded me of the pioneers of the early days, in the nineties, in Manitoba-kind-hearted folk, full of hopefulness, looking to the future with optimism, and believing they had the best country under the sun. To me it was a most pleasing experience to go back into that country, far up in the north, and see the splendid crops being raised there.
I should like to have said a few words in regard to some of the different schemes we have, but I am forced to pass on seeing that my time is going rapidly. I think we have covered nearly all the recommendations made by the committee on agriculture which investigated the Immigration department last year. We have extended assistance to boys between the ages of seventeen and nineteen inclusively. As most hon. members know, these boys are going to farm centres established by the different provinces. The province establishes a farm centre, or what may be called a distribution point, to which the boys go. Places are found for them by the provincial governments, and the Dominion contributes $10, the province $10, and the Imperial government $20, making a total of S40 per boy, for the purpose of placing him when he comes to Canada.

The provinces have undertaken to look after the boys, keeping an eye on them, and seeing that they are properly cared for after arriving. This is the most successful movement in a small way I have
The Budget-Mr. Forke

seen since coming to the department. I have heard nothing but good repots with respect to the placing of the boys who come to the country, and this is the best kind of immigration we can have. These lads come to Canada, become identified with Canadian life and social customs, and in a very few years they will be Canadians in every sense of the word, looking on the country as their own home land.
The committee also recommended a land settlement scheme, in respect to which there was a tripartite agreement between the provinces, the Dominion and the Imperial government. That has been done more particularly in New Brunswick and, to some extent, in Ontario. New Brunswick is advancing rapidly in the matter of land settlement from the provincial point of view. The authorities there intend to settle 500 families in the next three years. They settled 100 families last year and they seem to be doing very well. The province provides the land, the Imperial government advances the money, and the Dominion government renders services to further the scheme. I may say, in regard to domestic servants, that we have entered into an agreement with the Imperial government. They have established centres for the training of domestic girls coming to the Dominion, and these girls are given six weeks' training. We have a lady officer attached to the Department of Immigration and she is over in Great Britain, seeing what training the girls are receiving, and satisfying herself that they will be suitable to Canadian homes. She will have the selection of the girls who come. The province taking any girl who comes from overseas undertakes to contribute $10 towards the upkeep of the central home. This is one aspect of immigration in respect to which the department can never fill the demands made upon it; it cannot supply all the domestic servants asked for.
Now I will say a few words with reference to land settlement generally. We have read some very alluring descriptions of the vast open spaces of the Dominion, millions of acres of fertile land waiting for people to come and cultivate it; and we have read about unemployed people in Great Britan. We are told that if only we would bring these unemployed people to Canada and place them in these vacant spaces the whole face of the country would be transformed, there would be smiling homesteads, happy and contented homes, and everything would go well. It seems quite eiasy to talk that way, but anyone who has ever had any associa-

tion with land settlement, with the bringing of people to this country and settling them on the soil, knows that the problem is not so easy as all that. It -is much more difficult than one might readily suppose who had never come -into contact with that sort of work. I notice that the Hon. Mr. Perrault, speaking in the Quebec legislature, made the following statement:
It is not the fault of the province if young men show no desire to rush to the colonization areas and build up from the beginning. The fault rather lies in the desire of the younger men to gather in the centres, despite the advantages offered by the government.
It is -the same old story: you can put people on the land, but it is a different job to keep them there. It is largely a question of remuneration, a question also of making rural life as attractive as it ought to be. Mr. Perrault adds:
Yet, within the past fifteen years, the government of Quebec has succeeded in establishing 50 new parishes in the province.
That is not so bad for the old province of Quebec in the way of land settlement endeavour. Frankly, I am not in favour of any land settlement that will burden the settler with large overhead expenses; it is better to begin slowly, gaining experience -and building up on a surer foundation. The amazing development that has taken place in western Canada did not come about by means of any great land settlement scheme; it was brought about by people beginning in a small way, humbly, adding to their belongings bit by bit until the whole country was transformed and now we find a population of 2,000,000 producing a tremendous amount of wealth-and this in one generation. That is the way development took place there; it was not brought about by the expenditure of millions of public money to induce people to go on the land.

There is one thing I have noticed in recent years, and that is the tendency of the farmers in the west to increase their holdings. A few years ago, when I first came to this house, I imagined that a change would take place, that the farms would be smaller units, the population more dense, and that some of the difficulties we were experiencing would disappear. The movement has been the other way, however; the farms are growing larger in the west rather than smaller. That is not the best thing for the country, but it is a fact. The improvement in machinery, with loss of man power,

The Budget-Mr. Forke
is resulting in a greater amount of produce.
I 'have an idea which perhaps might be worth considering: I wonder whether all this increase in production, with less man power, simply means paying for improved machinery.
I wonder whether those who are producing in very much larger volume, as a result of improved machinery, are very much the gainers after they have paid for the machinery they are buying. As I say, 'that is only an idea, but it is worth noting. There is this to be observed: In buying that machinery and creating that produce they have at least done a great deal towards stimulating industry and helping every other line of public endeavour in the Dominion. I want those people who perhaps are not so closely related to agriculture as I am to 'bear that in mind and to be always ready to do something to help the farmer in the struggle he is carrying on in a great industry.
Before leaving land settlement I wish to refer to the colonization department of the railways and other organizations and to touch upon what has been done by the different provinces. Before dealing with British immigration, however, I wish to make a few remarks in relation to foreign immigrants from what are known as non-preferred countries, although there is no such definition in the act or in the regulations. Some Hungarian gentlemen came to see me the other day and they felt that a slur was 'being cast upon them because they came from what we know as a non-preferred country. I wish to make it clear that there has never been any intention that any reflection should be cast on anyone. Indeed, in some respects, countries which are nominally non-preferred are in reality preferred countries, because there has been a more vigorous campaign for immigrants there than anywhere else in Europe.

To prevent misconception I want to pay a tribute to the people who have come from those countries. They have made contributions of permanent value to the life of the Dominion; they are talcing an active interest in Canadian problems and government, as witness members of local governments and one member of foreign birth in the Dominion parliament. They have worked in our lumber camps, helped to build our railways and highways, dug our ditches and given good service for wages received. They have cleared thousands of acres of our scrub land in the northern part of the prairie provinces and
have made the wilderness blossom as the rose. They have built their modest homes; in many instances they have every modern item of equipment on their farms and have purchased1 more machinery and equipment in recent years than other agriculturists, and they have added to the wealth of the country by the production of millions of dollars worth of farm produce. They have not lagged behind in other respects; they have sent their children to high schools and universities, fitting them as good citizens to take their part in thid young and growing nation.
Now I want to say a few words with regard to the situation in Great Britain as it affects immigration. The social and economic structure of Great Britain is not what it was in 1914; in fact all countries have changed greatly since that time. In 1914 there was no unemployment insurance, no sick benefits and no old age pensions, and most of the social legislation now considered important was non-existent. Agriculture was more important; strange to say, in twenty years a vast change has taken place in Great Britain with regard to agriculture. Then cars and motor trucks were little used, and that really has a great bearing on emigration to Canada. Young men were trained in the management of horses; practically all transportation with the exception of that carried on by railways was done by horses. That produced a very large number of young men skilled in handling and managing horses, but you cannot find those people in Great Britain to-day; they are driving motor trucks or engaged in some other work and they do not know anything about horses. That is a fundamental lesson they must learn when they are being trained for farm work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to address the house for a short time on some features of the financial statement presented to the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and then to deal with a few matters of particular interest to the province of Nova Sootia from which I come.
The outstanding feature of the budget, it seems to me, is the announcement that for the current fiscal year Canada wll have a revenue of $450,000,000. There are three extraordinary features about that announcement:	First, the enormous size of the
revenue ; second, the comparatively small population from which it is raised; third, the announcement comes after several years of drastic tax reductions. In periods of prosperity revenue is said to be buoyant, and I think it may well be said that Canada s revenues are buoyant at the present time; and this is the best evidence of the real fundamental prosperity of the country.	_
The existence of such large revenues raises an important question:	What should the
policy of the government be with respect to expenditures? Undoubtedly a great many people would welcome a policy of freer expenditures. In Halifax we have a paper which at the present time is advocating freer expenditures on the part of 'the government. This paper says:
Let posterity carry some of the burden assumed by this generation in the name of posterity.
In other words, there is opposition to these huge surpluses being applied to the reduction of the national debt. But it appears to me that if any hon. member bad a business which was heavily mortgaged, and consequently his interest charges were burdensome, he would in times of prosperity attempt to cut down his mortgage and interest charges. Therefore in my view the policy of the Minister of Finance in budgetting for large surpluses, and applying those surpluses to the reduction of the national debt in these periods of prosperity, is the proper policy for the national welfare. And we have the welcome announcement that the bonds amounting to $60,000,000, which will fall due in August 1929, will be retired out of surplus revenues, thus reducing the annual interest charge by $3,300,000.
There is a second feature of the budget which I think calls for passing notice. I refer to the substantial reduction of the sales tax. Speaking for myself, and I think for my constituents, I am glad that the sales tax .s being reduced instead of the income tax. Some newspapers give the impression that the IMr. A. M. Edwards.]
only opposition to any reduction in the income tax comes from western Canada. Well, I come from the east, and I think that I am reflecting the opinions of my constituents when I say that it is better to get rid of the sales tax before we begin to reduce the income tax any further. I do not blame the government for not wiping out the sales tax at once. I have listened to the arguments of the opposition during the last two sessions urging that the sales tax should be eliminated entirely; but the answer given by the Minister of Finance, that when great reductions in this tax take place there is -a shrinkage in the value of retail stocks, which may very possibly give rise to claims against the government for compensation, appears to me to be a convincing one. The sales tax should be reduced by degrees and eventually eliminated, and that is the policy which the government of the day is following.
There is a third feature of the budget to which I Miould like to refer, and that is the almost entire absence of any change either upward or downward in the tariff. There are a few tariff reductions and, I believe, one tariff increase, to meet a particular situation. There will be in the country, of course, some disappointment; many persons who would like to have the tariff increased, as for instance the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me, and some of the members from other constituencies in Nova Scotia will be disappointed because there are no tariff increases. On the other hand there are some members of the house who are disappointed because there have not been more drastic tariff reductions. But we should always bear in mind the great difficulties which any government of Canada has to face in adjusting the tariff so as to meet conditions in all parts of the Dominion, The Dominion of Canada is of such vast extent, and has so many industries, that the interests of one industry in one part of the country are very likely to conflict with the interests of another industry in another part; and what would benefit one, so far as tariff changes are concerned, would injure another. And not only is that true, but very often the interests of one industry in one part of the Dominion are not identical with the interests of the same industry in another part of the Dominion. One of the most interesting examples (bf that is the recent instance of two applications before the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation, one by the coal operators of British Columbia, asking for the abolition of all duties on coal, and another by the coal operators of Nova Sootia asking that certain drawbacks be

The Budget-Mr. Jlsley
eliminated, which would be in effect an increase or rather a restoration of duties on coal. That instance of conflict of interest between different branches of the coal industry itself shows very clearly the great difficulty which the government of Canada has in framing a satisfactory tariff policy. And what is true of the coal industry is to a certain extent also true of the fruit industry.
I of course come from a fruit growing constituency, and therefore I have listened with more than ordinary interest to the references which have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite to the needs and requirements of the fruit-growing industry. A great many members on the Conservative side of the house have urged that the fruit industry in Canada is not adequately protected at the present time, and that the course of the government is quite clear; they suggest that the government should give additional protection to the fruit industry. Now, because I know something about the fruit industry I should like to discuss that matter from the standpoint, first, of Canada as a whole, and then from tire standpoint of the province of Nova Scotia. One would perhaps think, after listening to the discussions in the house, that the fruit industry existed only in one part of Canada, or perhaps in two sections of the country, British Columbia and Ontario. But I would remind hon. members that there aire three fruit-growing areas in Canada, one in British Columbia, one in Ontario, and one in Nova Scotia. And in a normal year the fruit area of Nova Scotia produces more fruit than does either of the other areas.

So far as cheapness of production is concerned, it requires only a moment's

There are those who say that we are turning more to the Canadian market than formerly, and that may possibly be so. What are these tariff requirements of which I speak? Generally speaking, they are that the tariff should seek a low level rather than a high level. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCLAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with deep interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) this afternoon, and I think I can sincerely say that his exposition and portrayal of the fruit possibilities and potentialities in the province of Nova Scotia was a very lucid and striking one. The hon. member is thoroughly conversant with that phase of industry in Nova Scotia, and his handling of

the matter this afternoon is worthy of at least some little tribute. I do not know that I can compliment the hon. gentleman, however, on his handling of the financial affairs of the Dominion of Canada, not with respect to the figures but in connection with the statement he made that in an affluent condition a farmer who had his farm mortgaged would naturally want to set aside a certain amount each year when conditions were encouraging in order to retire the obligation as soon as possible. Well, Mr. Speaker, for some two years past we have contended from this side of the house that the government with their enormous surpluses should be setting aside a certain amount of money annually in order to retire the national debt within a specified number of years, be it thirty, forty or fifty. And while I am on the question of the overflowing treasury, may I say that if the Dominion government feels so affluent with the resources it has at its command and the revenue it is receiving from the people of the Dominion of Canada, it might well exercise some measure of generosity towards the provinces of the Dominion, some of which are struggling very hard in order to make both ends meet. I speak particularly in this connection with respect to the province of Nova Scotia.
Might I mention here that very recently there has been submitted to the government of the province of Nova Scotia an interim report by the commissioner who was appointed to investigate an old age pension scheme in that province, and he has estimated in this report, which is not at all complete, that the total cost to inaugurate such a scheme-of which, I might say, every person in the province of Nova Scotia is heartily in favour-will amount to $4,400,000, the portion to be borne by the province to be $2,200,000, plus the expense of the administration of the scheme. If there is an overflowing treasury, as has been intimated by many of the members on the other side of the house who have spoken, I think it might well be applied in this direction, so that some of our struggling provinces may be able to put into force some such social legislation as the old age pensions scheme.
The bon. member for Han'ts-Kings also stated that he was glad to see a reduction in the sales tax. Naturally we are all glad, but the reduction does not go far enough. We advocated last session, as we do now, that the sales tax should be abolished, that on such necessities as wearing apparel and boots and shoes particularly the burden of taxation should not be left on the backs of those least able to bear it. We maintain

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
that the sales tax should be abolished, and there is every reason for the Minister of Finance to take this action. The hon. member expressed the opinion that it would not be wise to abolish the tax immediately for reasons he stated. If I remember correctly, Mr. Speaker, from this side of the house last session it was advocated that a specific date be fixed on which the sales tax would be abolished. Had our suggestion been adopted the shrinkage in retail values which the hon. gentleman put forward as an objection to the abolition of the sales tax would have been avoided, and the matter could have become effective without disrupting business.
He also said that there were a great many lamentations from this side of the house over the refusal of the government to implement in toto the recommendations of the Dunoan report. I well remember, sir, when, in the session of 1926, those of us who came from Nova Scotia presented the needs of the maritime provinces, we were taunted from the other side of the house as being calamity-howlers and peddlers of gloom, and similar epithets were hurled at us; but the investigation conducted by the Duncan commission proved that we were not far astray in the claims we made at that time, and the final report fully justified the position we had taken. Therefore it does not seem to me to ibe appropriate now to accuse us of being calamity-howlers.
Now, with respect to the boasted prosperity of the country, as the hon. member stated, there is a certain amount of prosperity in the province of Nova Scotia. He mentioned Halifax particularly, and I do not think it can be denied that there has been an improvement cf conditions at that port; there is a good deal of work going on there to-day. Nor can it be denied that there is some degree of prosperity in different portions of the Dominion, but, as he pointed out, that prosperity for the most part is confined to the larger centres. It is quite true that the banks are bursting with money, and it is also true that .the coffers of the insurance companies are overflowing with funds. It may be true that the millionaires are becoming multi-millionaires; but the real test of prosperity is not that the rich are getting richer, and the poor poorer, but that the working people are better off. Unless our national prosperity can stand that test, I do not think it is appropriate for the government to become so insistent about the much heralded prosperity the Dominion is enjoying under their administration; and I submit that the contrary is the fact Only the other evening
the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) cited specific instances of poverty and suffering in his city. Indeed, this unfortunate condition prevails in isolated places all over Canada. I believe there is a measure of spotted prosperity, but it is not a genuine prosperity, for it does not touch the people who most need it, the ones we want to make prosperous-the poor people.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in a brilliant speech teeming with facts severely castigated the government for its neglect to adopt means to properly safeguard and protect agricultural and industrial life in Canada, and moved an amendment regretting their failure. In supporting the amendment I do not propose to detain the house at any great length. I associate myself most heartily with the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) protesting against the failure of the government to implement in full the recommendations of the Duncan report. In this protest he is not only speaking his own mind and the minds of the members from the maritime provinces on this side of the house, but he is expressing also the sentiment of all the people of those provinces. The government appointed the Duncan commission, in due course the commission made its report; the government presented it to this house, and it was received with absolute approval by all hon. members. That was about two years ago. Lest there be any misunderstanding with respect to where the government stand in this connection, I may recall to the minds of hon. members some of the statements made by certain ministers. First let me quote the Prime Minister. Speaking in this chamber on January 31, 1928, he said:
The government at the present time has implemented a very considerable part of the report, and we intend to continue to carry out its recommendations.
That was well over a year ago. Now I come to the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). Speaking in St. John on January 18, 1928, he is reported in the Fredericton Daily Gleaner of the following day in these terms:
The federal government's policy with regard to the Aralley railway and the matter of a bounty to the Sydney steel plant would be divulged in a few weeks in a manner that would make every maritimer proud, according to a statement made on Wednesday night by Hon. Dr. P. J. Veniot, Postmaster General, at a banquet tendered in his honour by the Liberals of the constituency of St. John-Albert. All the other recommendations of the Duncan report had been implemented, he said.
On December 1, 1927, speaking at a banquet in the town of Amherst, tendered in his

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
honour, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is reported in the Halifax Chronicle next day as follows:
Mr. Ralston told of the long cabinet meetings when the Duncan report was being considered, and quoted the statement of Premier King at that time: "I have told the people of the maritime provinces that I have asked this commission to make specific recommendations in order that we might apply specific remedies, and I regard the carrying out of these recommendations as a matter of honourable obligation to the citizens of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island."
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is the slightest dispute as to where the government stand with respect to implementing the recommendations contained in the Duncan report. They have gone on record as being in favour of implementing those recommendations in toto. That has not been done; there are some major considerations and recommendations that have not been dealt with up to the present time. We want to know from the government when they intend to implement in full not only those recommendations, but also their solemn pledges given to the people of the maritime provinces on the floor of this house and on almost every public occasion in the maritime provinces when members of the cabinet have dealt with the report.
While I am on that subject I would direct the attention of the house to the report of the Duncan commission, page 36, section 23, with reference to the customs tariff on coal. I quote the following:
Several features of the customs tariff in its relation to coal were brought to our attention both by the government of Nova Scotia and by the operators of the coal mines. These rve feel ourselves precluded from dealing with, since they are a matter properly to be considered by the tariff advisory board; but we may be permitted to say that we are impressed with the need for reconsideration of the customs tariff in its relation to the coal industry and coke, and we recommend that the tariff advisory board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the subject.
I would now ask the Minister of Finance whether the tariff board has ever been asked by this government to give immediate consideration to the matter. I pause for an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCLAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my hon. friend well knows, the inquiry has been in progress before the board for some time, and the people in the maritime provinces are some of them divided among themselves as to what they should have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCLAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are not in the least divided. Two applications have

been before the board, one from the Orows-nest Coal Company in British Columbia, and the other from Besco in Nova Scotia; but that has absolutely nothing to do with the recommendation in the Duncan report requesting the government to ask the tariff board to investigate the matter. Will the Minister of Finance now give me a direct answer to a direct question. Has the government ever asked the tariff board to consider the question of a tariff on coal and steel? I do not think the government has ever asked the tariff board to consider the question. It is true that Besco has asked, and it is also true that the Crowsnest Company in British Columbia has requested consideration of a reduced tariff on coal. But so far as I know there has been no reference from this government to the tariff board.
The minister has spoken of some differences of opinion with respect to the matter. It is true that when the bounty question came up they wanted to postpone the hearing in order to have the government of Nova Scotia represented. But the Premier of Nova Scotia properly said: "This is a settled question. This matter has been settled by the Duncan commission and there is absolutely no necessity for us to reopen something that has already been decided by a board with at least coequal jurisdiction with the tariff advisory board." That is why the government of Nova Scotia would have nothing to do with the investigation in that connection; the matter had been settled and settled satisfactorily to the people of Nova Scotia. Not only that, but ministers of the crown had promised that the settlement in accordance with the recommendations contained in the Duncan report would be made. The government of Nova Scotia would have been putting itself in a most anomalous position if it appeared before the tariff board and asked to have something reconsidered when it had already been considered in their favour, having as a matter of fact been unanimously approved by this parliament and promised by the government. This is one recommendation at least which the government has totally ignored. Let me again quote the exact language of the report:
And we recommend that the tariff board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the subject.
This report has been in the hands of the government for over two years. I do not know that I need stress further the question of implementing the Duncan report except to say this: the people have been waiting a considerable time to have the ques-

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
tion properly disposed of. Two years ago, when the government asked for some delay in the matter, many of the members on this side of the house were generous enough, if I may use that expression, to get up and assure them that they would not press the administration at that time, inasmuch as they thought that some little time should be afforded in which to implement the recommendations. We were very glad to make that statement on the floor of the house. But we have waited two years and there is in the budget nothing which intimates that any remedy will be provided as recommended. We are now therefore at the point of vigorous protest. You may call it calamity howling, if you will; you may call us peddlers of gloom or anything you wish. But we are here to perform a duty and so long as we are here we will be heard.
Now I want to deal for a minute or two with the coal industry in Nova Scotia. It is true that there has been a little improvement in the coal fields in that province, due I think, in large measure, to the very capable manner in which the provincial government has handled the mines of the province. There have not been any labour troubles since the Rhodes government came into power. The Minister of Mines is a man of outstanding capacity and ability and he has skilfully guided the affairs of the coal interests in Nova Scotia, so that they have been in a more or less happy position ever since that government assumed power. Nevertheless there is still room for improvement in conditions there. There is opportunity for a larger output of coal in Nova Scotia, provided we can secure the market; and the only way to secure the market is by means of some assistance from this government. Whether it be by lower freight rates, whether it be by tariff measures, whether it be by subventions, whether it be by some system of bonus or by any other means, there is, I say, chance for increased production of coal in Nova Scotia provided we secure the market. I know there are many difficulties in the way of the application of the tariff in its relation to the coal industry, but I am not by any means abandoning what I have always maintained to be one of the things necessary to help the industry, namely, a higher tariff on coal. I have heard a slur cast across the floor of the house many times, but I do not think there is any disagreement, so far as the members on this side of the house are concerned, with respect to properly and adequately protecting every legitimate industry in this Dominion. That has always been the stand of the Conservative party, and that policy has never
been abandoned by that party so far as I am able to ascertain. That being the case, there is no reason in the world why the Dominion Fuel Board, constituted by this government, and on which there are many officials, should not be broadened out in scope so that it might be able to bring in proper recommendations to the government as to the best way in which to develop a national fuel and steel policy for this Dominion. No effort has been made by the fuel board along this line. The board costs the country about
120,000	per annum. I have nothing to say with regard to the personnel of the board; they are all capable and efficient men. But they all have other duties to perform, and their work in connection with the Dominion Fuel Board occupies only their spare time. It is incumbent upon the government, if they are not able to cope with the situation themselves-and there is clear evidence that they are not able to cope with it-to place the matter in the hands of some commission or other authority who will work out sooner or later-sooner, we hope-some sort of fuel policy for Canada which will be of benefit not only to the coal interests of the Dominion, to the coal miners, but generally to all the people of the country. We do not know how long it will be before some crisis may overtake us. And we do not want to be dependent upon any country for any staple article such as coal, which is one of the necessities of life. If a big strike should take place in the United States, where we purchase about 17,000,000 tons of coal of different kinds every year, most of it the very kind of coal we can produce in Canada, and if in consequence we were some day unexpectedly shut off from that market-and that might happen -then we should be in a hopeless and helpless position with regard to one of the very necessities of life. I say that I do not believe proper consideration has been given the fuel question in this Dominion, and it is up to this government to place the matter in the hands of some properly constituted board or commission, and have that body develop some scheme and bring in some recommendation which will help solve this great problem. When it is solved, Mr. Speaker, you may rest assured that it will materially help the people of the province of Nova Scotia, one-fifth of whom are dependent upon the coal industry.
Not only has this government not given proper consideration to the coal industry of Canada, but I want to refer to a matter which I brought up last year. When the Canadian National Railways were consolidated, part of the assets of the Grand Trunk consisted of a coal mine in the United States,

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
operated by a company known as the Rail and River Coal Company, and the Canadian National Railways have been operating that company in the United States for several years past. The company employes about 700 men, and according to the labour organizations of the United States the mine is being operated in an improper manner. There is no union labour employed at that mine; they use the cheapest kind of labour and do not recognize 'the labour unions. Just here I wish to quote a letter from a high official of the United Mine Workers of America. I do not wish to give the name of this official, but if anyone is interested I shall be glad to show him the correspondence a little later. The letter states:
The Rail and River Coal Company prior to April 1, 1927, operated its mines under the joint agreement with the United Mine Workers of America and up until that time recognized the principles of collective bargaining in its dealings with the organization chartered by the American labour movement and having jurisdiction throughout the mines of America.
And further:
They have operated these mines for some months now and have never signified any intentions of recognizing the United Mine Workers, but seemingly are willing to deal with a group associated under a leadership in this vicinity who, because of their communistic doctrines have in some instances been refused by the authorities in this section, to hold meetings, it having been assumed by the authorities due to literature that was distributed, that this element was opposed to our form of government.
Referring to the United Mine Workers of America, I presume.
One would think that the Canadian government owning and operating a railroad which in turn operates mines, would at least use a system in the operation of its mines that reflects ideals and principles; namely, collective bargaining in their dealings with their employees in the mines and that they should not deal with a group whose aim has been to obstruct the United Mine Workers of America which has always been a part of the system of collective bargaining.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time the management of the Canadian National Railways were instructed by this house not to violate the established principles of labour as followed by the United Mine Workers of America; and to see that the men employed in these mines belong to labour unions and receive the consideration which these unions are always so generous to give their members.

In the same
way that it affects the swine industry; poultry thrive on the by-products of the dairy industry. I should think the hon. member, coming from the part of the country he does, would know all about that. Not only have the dairymen's associations passed these resolutions, but the farmers' associations have asked this government to abrogate that part of the treaty which applies to New Zealand. It has been estimated that over 20,000,000 pounds of butter have been dumped on the Canadian market during the past year. Their seasons are exactly the opposite to ours; it is summer time in New Zealand at the present time, there is a rich carpet of feed for the animals and it is impossible for the farmers in the part of the country from which I come to meet that unfair competition. At this time of the year the cattle in our country require shelter and are simply eating their heads off, while the cattle in New Zealand are roaming around the fields at very little cost, and their butter is thrown on our market under the added advantage of a bonus. It does not seem to me that it is fair to an industry such as the dairy industry to have to work under such a disadvantage. There are but a few branches of agriculture in Nova Scotia which can compete with the other countries of the world, and I do not think the dairy industry comes within that category, under existing conditions.
We could not compete with the western meat trade, but it was thought that we would be able to compete in the dairy business. The farmers established dairy herds all over the

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
province. They began to prosper as a result of the development of those herds, combined with the business in swine which was built up as a by-industry. When New Zealand butter began to swamp the market the farmers discovered that they could not compete and decided they would have to dispose of their herds. When they do that they practically abandon the whole farming industry in our province, because that is about the only profitable phase of it left. I ask the members of the house whether they think it is a proper attitude for any government to take to continue to allow this New Zealand butter to come in and flood our markets and put the Nova Scotia farmers out of business. Resolutions have been sent to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) from agricultural societies and institutions throughout the whole Dominion, and it seems to me that some attention should be given to this matter. I believe the Australian treaty has been of great help to certain parts of Canada, but 1 protest against that part of the treaty which allows New Zealand butter to come in under an order in council which was passed without the matter having been discussed on the floor of this house. On behalf of the farmers of Nova Scotia I appeal to the government to give this matter their attention. It is one that is worthy of their notice, and if they knew the conditions which actually exist in the maritime provinces I believe it would have their immediate attention, that is necessary if those conditions are to be remedied.
It is only idle talk to contend that the proposals in the budget form an adequate substitute for the recommendations of the Duncan commission. The coal and steel industry requires a duty sufficiently adequate to safeguard and protect it. It needs a $2 per ton test rate on coal from Cape Breton and Nova Scotia to the Montreal market. A delegation came to Ottawa a short time ago and put this matter before the government. A test rate of $3 per ton was placed on the movement of coal, and while it served some purpose i't was found that it was not low enough to enable any great quantity of Nova Scotia coal to seek the present markets and develop new ones. We urge the government to give consideration to the matter of a $2 test rate on the movement of coal from Nova Scotia. We want to see our Canadian coal used in coking plants. The Domestic Fuel Act as it stands to-day is absolutely worthless so far as the use of Canadian coal is concerned. Outside of one small plant in the city of Halifax, Canadian coal is not being used in any cok-
ing plant in Canada. They are not taking advantage of the provisions of the Domestic Fuel Act. I was amazed no>t long ago when I heard a patriotic appeal to the citizens of the Dominion of Canada which was sent over a certain broadcasting station, they were asked to buy a certain grade of coke on the plea that they would be patronizing home industry and helping to build up Canada. But there was one thing they overlooked, and that was to tell the audience that the coke manufactured at this plant was being made of American bituminous coal, coal that could have been supplied from our own mines.
