speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) will not blame me if I do not follow him in his argument. He was dealing solely with Nova Scotia problems and the dear old Duncan report; I propose to speak on the budget, which is the matter supposed to be under debate in the house.
The budget and the debate which has followed upon it have raised larger issues than are contained in the terms of the budget. It has awakened a realization in the minds of some of the hon. members opposite that this is a glorious opportunity to put the principle of protection on the lexicon of the agriculturists from the west. It has also put the fear in the minds of some of the farmers, low tariff men and free [traders, that they might 'be affected by this false and emotional doctrine. The budget itself is a very harmless instrument so far as I am concerned. I personally have not uplifted my voice to say, nor has my heart been satisfied, that the provisions contained in the budget will alleviate the burdens of those I represent. I am safe in saying that the budget is absolutely inactive to those of my way of thinking, and the only morsel of satisfaction I get from it is that there have been no additional burdens placed upon us. I realize that the possible outcome of the situation in the United States has had its effect; nevertheless I state to this house that despite what may or may not be done by the United States there are certain things which might well be done by this parliament.
I am very thankful that there has been no reduction in the income tax. I with others last year strongly urged that no reduction should take place in the income tax. I took then, as I do now, the broad general prin-cipile that no further reductions should be made in the income tax until the war debt has been brought to a point where it can be reasonably expected to be paid out of consolidated revenue. The Minister of Finance

The Budget-Mr. Glen
(Mr. Robb), in his admirable statement, showed that this debt took 42.30 per cent of our revenue. Surely the country has a right to expect that those who are sharing in the largest degree the unprecedented prosperity which all members of the house are speaking of, shall make their contributions undiminished under this tax. The loss of revenue by any reduction will have to be made up somehow, and my fear is that when that time comes, it will be by way of indirect taxation. Some say that the farmers would benefit by a reduction. We had an enormous crop in 1928 and we had a great crop in 1927, but I find that for the year 1927-28 only 291 farmers in Manitoba were able to pay income tax, and I shall be surprised if that number is appreciably increased for 1928-29. It has been pointed out several times during the course of the debate, and I would like to emphasize it from my knowledge, that the margin between profit and loss in last year's farming operations is so meagre and negligible that if there is a bad crop in 1930, hundreds of farmers are likely to become bankrupt. I do not think that is an exaggerated statement. From my personal knowledge I have a good acquaintance with the affairs of many farmers in Manitoba, and I know whereof I speak.
But having spoken thus of the budget, to which I will come back, I should like to refer to the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). If only its merit had been as admirable as the form in which it was presented, it would have been irresistible, but the subject matter of my hon. friend's speech was simply an appeal and argument for his point of view in favour of protection. The hon. member for South Wellington is too intelligent to advance the argument that .protection could benefit the producer. He knows, if anyone does, that a duty on wheat, which is largely exported, cannot give increased prices to the producer. His amendment must therefore be considered as relating to those whom I might term industrialists. The hon. gentleman's views and mine on that point are as far apart as the poles. There may be room for argument between us with regard to our viewpoint on protection to the industrialist, but there is no argument that a duty on wheat can give increased prices to the producer. Differing, therefore, as I do from the hon. member in the fundamentals of his argument, I must vote against the amendement.
I said in the beginning I thought the budget might have given some remedial relief, and I will instance two commodities which might have been mentioned in the budget. I refer to 78594-84
aluminum and enamelware. These two industries had hearings before the tariff board; they were investigated very thoroughly, and there was in my judgment indisputable evidence presented before the board that a reduction in the tariff on those commodities would be of considerable benefit to the consumer and no detriment to the manufacturer One or two statements have been made in the house somewhat derogatory to the tariff board. Any derogation of the work of the tariff board should in the first instance have come from those who appeared before it, and my information is that manufacturers and all others who have appeared before the board are at one in their sense of the fairness and equity which have been meted out to them in all the hearings. I believe sincerely it is a necessary forum in order to bring out the facts, and the only persons who fear the tariff board are those who do not wish to present their facts in public.
I should like to give one illustration of the effect of what the tariff board has done. Some time ago the Ottawa correspondent of the Manitoba Free Press made a very exhaustive and splendid report of the activities of the Canada Cement Company, and this was published in the Manitoba Free Press. That was followed by an application presented to the board by Mr. A. E. Darby of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. A splendid brief was submitted by Mr. Darby and an equally good response was made by Professor Jackson on behalf of the cement companies. The hearing took place and the issue was keenly fought. The results have not been embodied in the budget, but on the day following the introduction of the budget by the Minister of Finance there was published throughout the Dominion of Canada an intimation from the Canada Cement Company that the price of their goods was reduced ten cents per barrel and in many places fifteen cents per barrel. That reduction which is in some cases thirty per cent and in others fifty per cent of the present duty, on cement, is, I think, attributable to the light of publicity that was given before the tariff board and is as creditable to the cement company as it is to the advocates and to the board itself.
In justification of the reductions in the tariff and in support of the contention that reduced tariffs will provide more employment, I should like to suggest to the government that the present policy of lower tariffs is the policy most suitable for business within the boundaries of Canada. Most of us will remember the direful forebodings that were expressed last session on the budget by hon. gentlemen opposite and in particular, if I

The Budget-Mr,. Glen

remember aright, the hon. and genial member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) was the gloomiest prophet of all. I listened very carefully to his speech the other day and I certainly expected he would come forward with some illustrations showing that his forebodings were true and that his "I told you so" was correct. But I was disappointed; not a single instance did he give to bear out the prophecy which he made during last session. All he gave was his desire-and I presume as a medical man he is entitled to it-to see the red blood of somebody. He likes red and I venture to submit that he is seeing red just now. It happens that in the United States they have a board that is called the committee of ways and means, House of Representatives, and before that board the manufacturers and the people who are desirous of getting tariffs raised, appear and give evidence, I was very much struck, and I think the house will be somewhat surprised to hear this. On January 30, in their committee's prints, page 4449, is the evidence given by the mayor of the city of Lawrence, Massachusetts. This is rather striking in view of all that has been said with regard to employment in the United States and how that highly protected country is the best country in the world in which to live. Lawrence is a city of 94,000 people, situated about twenty-six miles north of Boston and as many miles from the Atlantic seaboard. The present mayor, after giving a picture of the city and its attractions, has this to say:
Gradually our mills have been going on shorter time and though we have been optimistic relief has not come. It has been said that from 10,000 to 20,000 people have left the city and none arrived to keep up our population. And may I say cotton and wollen mills do not pay a very high rate of wages and in the dull times the reserve fund of the operative is soon exhausted. I have shown this committee a gradual falling off of valuation for tax purposes about one and a half million in 1928 and perhaps another one and a half million in 1929, which is a direct loss to the city in income at our rate of $26.40 per 1,000 (the second lowest for cities in Massachusetts), $79,200. Not this alone but the closing of a mill such as the United States Worsted Company, which employed 1,500 workers, the Pemberton Mills (cotton) which employed 500; Lawrence Duck Company (cotton) employed 500, the Everett Mills with from 1,600 to 2,000 employed, the Katama with 300 employed; making in all 4,500 workers out of employment.
Then he goes on to say:
It puts a very heavy burden upon our charity and soldiers' relief departments. There are about 450 vacant stores and 2,300 vacant tenements in our city, so it is again the vicious circle. Mills close down or run on short time, merchants and storekeepers, landlords unable to 
collect and city handicapped in collection of taxes. I realize that tariff schedules and fixing of rates is work of and for experts, which I am not. The members of this committee know far more than I about this tariff. I am not sure that the remedy for the ills of the textile centers of the country is in further adjustment, of rates. I am not sure that the evil which has crept in to this great industry is due as some say to an overproduction of cotton and woollen goods; that there are too many spindles in operation; or that it is due to the investment of American money in the mills of foreign countries, where living conditions are lower and wages lower than in this country, or to the tariff. I am willing to be guided by the national organization experts of cotton and woollen trade, as the leading manufacturing men of our city are in harmony with these men who have made an exhaustive study of this situation. Yet when I see thousands of men and women, good, law-abiding, God-fearing people in my home city walking the streets unemployed; when I see the home that has been acquired and gained by the life work of the father of a family and his sons and daughters, slipping out of his grasp, I turn for assistance to every harbour. I cannot see a community that has progressed for seventy-five years bleed to death without lifting my voice in protest. These things should not be in this richest country in the world. I earnestly ask this committee, not for one instant putting my judgment above yours, to give cities like Lawrence, Lowell, New Bedford, and Fall River relief from these burdens. The people cry out in their anguish; cry out for work and an opportunity to earn a livelihood; to rear their families and pay their debts. If the remedy is in the tariff, as many say it is, I trust this committee will apply this cure, correct, and counteract the evil that exists.
I wonder where these forty-five hundred unemployed went. Just let us read a little further on. This is in the form of question and answer:

Mr. Landers is mayor of Lawrence:
-may I ask you if the authorities, like yourself, as mayor of Lawrence, have endeavoured to locate where your population has moved?
Mr. Landers:	Yes. We have tried that.
Mr. Treadway:	Do you know where they
have gone? What percentage of the total population lias left Lawrence, for instance, in the past two years?
Mr. Landers:	The greatest percentage of
them went to Canada.

Canadians and went back over the line?
Mr. Landers:	Yes.

had they come down from Canada?
Mr. Landers:	No; they were citizens.

Mr. Landers:	Yes.
Mr. Treadway:	Did they move out permanently, or would they be glad to come back, do you think, if business braced up.
Mr. Landers:	There is no question about
that. Whenever business does increase in Lawrence, then we have a shortage of tenements.

were no empty tenements in Lawrence?

Mr. Landers:	No, sir.
Mr. Treadway:	When did the decrease

Mr. Landers:	About 1925 and 1926.
Mr. Treadway:	It was worse in 1927 than

Mr. Landers:	Yes.

Mr. Landers:	Yes, sir.
I am told that a textile factory is being built in. Fainrham, Quebec, this year, which fact has some relation to the tariff reductions of last year. But, what I wish to point out is that in the United States, this highly protected country which members on the other side so frequently point to, there is a condition of affairs in that city of Lawrence not paralleled in any city in Canada.
I should like, however, to point out several factors in connection with United States and Canadian tariffs which may be of interest, and which must be considered when dealing with our relations with our neighbours to the south. The United States is held up in this house as a highly protected country, and it is a highly protected country, yielding only to Spain in the height of its tariff walls. The United States is held up in this house constantly as being unfair to Canada, and its tariff walls against Canada are too high; much too high. Yet there are certain facts which must be recognized in connection with trade with the United States.
During this debate it has been held by some hon. gentlemen that Canada has not retaliated, has not built up its walls as high as those of the United States against this country; yet an analysis of the trade flowing between the two countries, taking the figures for 1926, shows that 74 per cent of the exports from Canada to the United States were free, while only 29 per cent of the imports from the United States States into Canada were not dutiable. If the average rate of duty on all imports is taken as a measure of protection, it will be found that for the years 1926-1927 this rate was 13 per cent for the United States and 15.4 per cent for Canada.
An examination of the free list of the two countries reveals certain similarities, and naturally certain contrasts. The core of each list is made up of raw materials, such, for example, as crude minerals, raw cotton, raw silk, tanning and dyeing materials, crude rubber and crude petroleum. In addition there are certain exotic food products, such as tea and coffee, which although dutiable in Canada on the theory that we need the revenue, are not equally dutiable in the United State1:.
785:4- 64J
It may be that we sometimes blame the United) States unjustly. Certainly we think of them as having a duty on everything that they produce if we produce it, and yet coal is on their free list; cement is on their free list, as well as planed boards and a number of other commodities. We think of them, however, as imposing a duty on these commodities, and there is a duty on them, but only as against countries that themselves impose a duty. In other words, we could have free access to the United States in these commodities under present conditions at least if we gave the United States free access of these commodities into Canada.
The United States has chosen to leave certain industries unprotected. That may seem strange to the members of this house. I do not mean raw materials; I mean manufactured products, such as newsprint, boots and shoes, leather, agricultural implements and binder twine. I wish to draw attention to the fact that only one of these products, binder twine, is unprotected in Canada, and I wish to point out also that our manufacturers are sending leather and newsprint in large quantities to the United States and taking advantage of the free market in that country. I do not know how long these commodities are going to remain on the free list of the United States, but I do know that a lot of the talk that has been heard in this house in the last few days as to "red-blooded action" is not likely to lead to their continuation on the free list, and if they disappear the manufacturers of this country who are engaged in export trade will know whom they have to blame for the closing of the United States market against them.
Comment has been made as to the disparity between our imports from the United States and those from the United Kingdom. I yield to no one in my desire that my adopted country shall trade with my mother country, and yet I cannot close my eyes to sound business practice, and the channels of trade that flow according to climatic conditions. I should indeed, be glad if we were able to buy our raw cotton within the British Empire. With all my heart I pray for the success of the British government in its effort to make the British Empire independent in its cotton supply. We have in India and in Africa the kind of climate that is needed but it takes many years of slow, patient work to lead the producers of these countries to selectivity in seeds, to proper method of cultivation, and to a proper cleaning of the raw cotton. Until such time as the British Empire is self-supporting in the matter of the raw materials we require in this country and
The Budget-Mr. Glen

which by reason of climatic conditions or otherwise, we cannot ourselves produce, then we must buy them from the country in which we can get them the cheapest, and that country often happens to be the United States.
We have heard a great deal about the iron and steel industry and the necessity of protecting it, and yet in a sense the iron and steel industry is exotic to this country. We are not making a pound of steel from Canadian ore. We import our ore, some of it, fortunately, from Newfoundland, but most of it from the United States. During the sessions of the tariff board the iron and steel producers from all over Canada were present and were asked if they favoured a duty upon iron ore, and none of them favoured a duty upon iron ore. They were business men. They wanted to buy their raw materials in the market which sold those materials at the lowest price, although that market happened to be the United States.
Once for all, let us recognize that we cannot, much as some of hon. members of this house would have us do so, copy the tariff clothes of the United States and expect to be suitably and well dressed. This country is different, geographically and climatically, from the United States. This country develops its natural resources, and tariff laws everywhere must adjust themselves to the conditions which it is proposed they shall serve; and, as a result of our limitations, the raw materials out of which are manufactured the necessities of life have frequently to be imported. Foreign trade is more important to the Dominion of Canada than it is to the United States. Now the United States, by reason of its high tariff, has also restricted its imports, and there is a growing feeling against a high tariff in the United States, despite what is said to the contrary. Leading economists there have indicated that this is likely to be the last high tariff congress in that country, because they realize that-their export trade is being diminished so appreciably by high tariffs that they will have to call a halt. As a matter of fact there is a good deal of laughter in the United States, on the part of those who know, with regard to the demands at present made in Washington. And the one thing which will kill any project is to laugh at it. The United States has become alarmed, seriously alarmed as a matter of fact, and if I had time I would read to you an extract from the report of the proceedings of the same committee. It is rather long however and I will therefore give the gist of it. It is this: that the exports to Cuba from the United States have been so tremend-

ousfy diminished as a result of the imposition of a high tariff against Cuban goods entering the United States that the economists of the United States are becoming very much alarmed indeed. In many cases, the goods formerly purchased from the United States by the Cubans are now reduced to a half and a third. That is the position with regard to the United States. I do not think that anyone can fail to understand why it is that we who represent the exporters of Canada-the industry which is responsible for most of the export trade of the country, the wheat industry-fear that it is likely to be throttled by high duties such as, if hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, would be imposed upon goods entering Canada; because high import duties in Canada would act as they have acted in the United States and everywhere else-they would shut out imports.
In closing I wish to say something on the doctrine of retaliation as preached by the Conservatives. I heard with dismay the other night the astounding proposal of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), that the government be given authority to make immediate tariff changes to meet any fiscal changes that may take place in the United States. I can hardly imagine that any responsible member on the Conservative benches would support or even countenance a proposal so preposterous. Let me say to the hon. member that I cannot understand how under any conceivable circumstances any western member would delegate to any government such an exclusive parliamentary privilege in connection with so contentious a subject as the tariff. Goodness knows, we have plenty of trouble meantime with the officials who presume to interpret our tariff regulations, without giving the government a blanket power as is suggested. I am quite sure that we shall hear something from the leader of the apposition (Mr. Bennett) when he speaks on this question. I can hardly imagine his being likely to countenance such a proposal.
If my reading of history is correct, I should say that, apart from religious wars, nearly all wars have had, as one of their primary causes, economic conditions. I was reading Henry Kittredge Norton's book, Back of War, and I want to quote therefrom one or two statements in support of the contention I make. At page 74 the author says:
It is not needful for us to go into the merits or demerits of protective tariffs. That they result in an intensification of the economic conflict between nations can hardly be disputed, and that is the aspect of the matter which interests us here. The general effect of the protective tariff system is that each nation, no matter how small, strenuously endeavours to

The Budget-Mr. Glen
become economically self-sufficient. No nation has ever succeeded in doing this. Even the United States, with a vast continent of unexampled resources and a considerable tropic [DOT] empire, is dependent upon outside sources for rubber, coffee, and a score of other essential raw materials and foodstuffs. Great Britain, with an even more extended and varied territory, is equally dependent upon other nations. The same is true of every other state, yet the effort goes on and each nation strives to increase the amount and variety of its own products, at no matter what economic loss to its own people.
The tariff is the chief and typical instrument by which this uneconmic competition is carried on. In most countries it has long since forgotten the "revenue" stage, and in many it has even passed the "protective" stage. It is frankly a "retaliatory" measure. A prohibitory tariff is erected against the products of a particular nation, either to penalize that nation or to be removed in return for special favours. Sometimes a general reduction is made on both sides by a "reciprocity" agreement. The tariff is a powerful weapon in the economic warfare which is prevalent to-day in peace times. When it is used ruthlessly and with sole regard to the advantage of the nation using it, or as a direct thrust at some other nation, it may well become an important factor in precipitating armed conflict.
And in one short paragraph he sums up his views thus:
War is not to be persuaded out of existence. Our only hope for an era of continued peace is to recognize and deal with the causes of international conflict. These are largely economic. They are not wholly so, and the economic cause is frequently overlaid with numerous layers of insulation made up of high-sounding protestations of patriotism, national honour, and national rights. It is the task of the sincere worker for world peace to cut through these outer layers and lay bare the real causes of dispute, and to demand that the statesmen of the world deal with these sanely and constructively.
If this is not a sufficient authority, I was looking at Norman Angell's book, Human Nature and the Peace Problem, and in it he gives two or three quotations from one of the leading journalists in the old country- I do not think one would be exaggerating if one said, the leading journalist-Mr. J. L. Garvin. Mr. Garvin is the author of a postwar book entitled The Economic Foundations of Peace, and its first chapter summary begins:
A primary war, largely about food and raw materials: inseparable connection of the politics and economics of the peace.
And his first paragraph contains the following:
The war with many names was in one main aspect a war about food supply and raw materials. To this extent it was Germany s fight to escape from the economic position of inter-independence without security into which she had insensibly fallen-to obtain for herself
independent control of an ample share in the world's supplies of primary resources. The war meant much else., but it meant this as well and. this wias a vital factor in its causes.
Now it is impossible to develop this theme in a forty minute speech, and it must wait therefore for another place and more leisure. But I view with a good deal of uneasiness the utterances of Conservative members of the house in this debate. Any dispute with the United States which is likely to take place in the future must come about over matters concerning commerce, trade or financial claims. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he was in the old country, made the proud boast that there wa3 between the two countries a boundary in which there was not a fort. Shall we begin a tariff wall against those people, with all the attendant dangers, suspicion and ill will? No one can deny or will deny that the United States have, as Canada has, the right to change their customs law; that is their inherent right as it is ours. Does ft not resolve itself simply into this, that if the United States do not wish to trade with us there is no other course for us to follow but to seek the markets of the world, and preferably of course the British market? I shall await with a good deal of interest the speech of the leader of the opposition, for I am quite sure that he will modify the mischievous utterances of many of his followers in this debate during his absence.
Now, one would naturally conclude that I must of necessity vote for the subamendment.
I think the subamendment need not have been introduced at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCLAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not try to emulate the eloquence of those hon. members who have immediately preceded me, but in my own small way I shall try to tell the house what I think of the budget. I was very much surprised to hear the last speaker (Mr. Glen) say that the budget was a harmless instrument, that in fact it was a negative instrument. I suppose he looks upon the budget very much in the same way that we used to look upon some old woman's medicine-if it did not help, it at least would not hurt. I was also rather surprised to hear him say that he was very glad that there were no reductions in the income tax. Well, some reductions were made in the income tax last session, but on that occasion the hon. gentleman did not show his dissatisfaction by his vote.
Now, the budget presented to the house by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will no doubt be heralded throughout the length and breadth of Canada by the friends of the Liberal party as a marvellous revelation of financial ingenuity, revealing as it does the great ability of the minister and his reputed *passion for economy. Right here, sir, in respect to this much talked-of economy, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance does not feel pretty much in the same position as his prototype of many centuries ago, who when questioned by the king of that day as to his happiness and contentment said:
I envy nobody, no not I,
And nobody envies me,
I owe no money I cannot pay;	.
I thank the river Dee
That turns the mill that grinds the corn To feed my babes and me.
But when I look into the eye of the minister and see that wistful look of sadness, I have to come to another conclusion.
The Liberals will also point with great pride to the unprecedented surplus of seventy million dollars, to a reduction in taxes, and also to a decrease in the national debt. But no mention will be made of any reduction in the tariff, as it will be found much better to leave well enough alone. One might easily 
argue that if the minister had not successfully gambled on future prosperity, in other words, if our field crops and the products of our forests, mines and factories had not produced so much wealth and thereby given our people more money with which to pay taxes, the result would not have been so satisfactory to him. But I am willing to give him the benefit of the doubt, and in so far as the sales tax and other nuisance taxes are concerned I shall go even to the length of extending to him my congratulations for the reductions made therein.
I wish to deal with three things, Mr. Speaker; first, the tariff; next, the railway situation; and, if I have any time left, certain phases of immigration. In respect to the tariff changes in this budget, having in view the alleged tariff policy of the Liberal party, I cannot very well see my way clear to offer any commendation to the government. The tariff changes in my opinion are completely negligible in that they offer no relief whatsoever to those engaged in agriculture, and the tariff resolutions that will follow this debate, while on their face they appear impressive, will be found after the calm reflection that usually follows a close analysis to mean but very little. They make free a few minor articles that are hardly ever used in this country, but in no shape or form do they affect any real industry one way or the other. In view, therefore, of the great divergence between Liberal promise and Liberal performance I cannot pass over my remarks on the budget without some appeal to the party to the right of the Speaker for a stricter adherence to the principles on which they were elected to parliament, for I fear if this is not done those engaged in agriculture will be placed in the same position as the polar bear perched on an iceberg which is gradually melting away as it approaches the equator.
It is not enough for the Minister of Finance to make the trite remark, "We are the only low tariff party in the House of Commons." Such a statement must be backed up by action, for actions speak louder than words. It is not the first time we have heard a member of the government do lip service with respect to a low tariff policy and we know it will not be the last; and, having this in mind, well do I remember the remark made by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. 'Evans) wherein he said that the Liberals, after dodging the tariff issue since confederation, experienced a softening of the heart inasmuch as they actually lowered the tariff in 1904 on soft soap and false teeth; and in 1929, after undergoing a similar psychological

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
change, the hon. Minister of Finance out of the goodness of his heart actually ran the terrible risk of lowering the duty on cocoa-nuts. "From false teeth to cocoanuts we lowered the duty on everything," might very well be the party slogan at the next election.
Now, from information I have gathered from expert sources, I have learned that since 1888 the difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives in respect to the tariff has been eight-tenths of one per cent in favour of the Liberals-a difference which in my estimation is nothing much to blow about. In view of this fact I would like to ask the government whether or not the tariff is an issue, and if it is an issue will the members of the government still claim to be the apostles of a lower tariff? Personally, Mr. Speaker, I feel like the man from Missouri;
I do not believe in any platitudinous humbug; I want the government to produce the goods, but have the government produced the goods? My opinion is emphatically in the negative.
I do not wish to burden this house with any statistics or voluminous references; I simply wish to give a review of the three years I have been in this house, which I think will be quite sufficient for my purposes. What happened here in 1927? So far as any revision of the tariff was concerned, absolutely nothing happened, and since one may find reasons for almost anything, so have the government found an alibi for their attitude in connection with the tariff. In that year the minister explained that there could be no revision until the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation had finished some oases which were before them. According to my information they did finish some cases that year, but the minister did not take account of those cases at all. Indeed, the only satisfaction wc received that year was what consolation we could take from the statement made by the Minister of Finance, as follows:
We shall move forward cautiously with the aid of the knowledge of the facts secured by the tariff advisory board towards the goal of making our tariff structure bear as lightly as possible on production, on industry and the people generally, having in view the greater prosperity of all legitimate industries of Canada. The tariff must be made to serve the best interests of the Canadian people as a whole. It must be adjusted from time to time bo meet the needs, not of one class or group of industries alone, whichever one that might be, but of our whole economic structure.
It is hard to conceive of a more carefully worded statement than the one I have just quoted and behind which the government have striven to remain so snugly secure. Nothing so irritates a bear as to be suddenly
awakened from his long winter sleep by a casual intruder, and I cannot imagine a more apt analogy than that of an aggressive member of this house piercing through the thin armour of the superficial apologetics of this statement made by the Minister of Finance. Certainly I cannot regard it as anything but an attempt on the part of the government to put a quietus on the policy of low tariff, in view of some of the disturbing elements on that side of the house. As I see it, the Liberal party is divided into three different parts; we have the Liberal party proper, who preach low tariff but never practise it; we have the Conservative-Liberals, who decry any low tariff whatsoever, and we have the Liberal-Progressives, who have been led into the party opposite by the astute Prime Minister of Canada under whose magic influences they have been lulled into blissful forgetfulness of the policies which brought them here in 1921. Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, it is very curious indeed what strange bed fellows politics do make.
So far as the budget of 1928 is concerned I think very few people in Canada understood what the items in the budget meant; they were chiefly concerned with the schedules of the textile industry, and the only clear thing about them was that they were in line with the policy of the government of reducing the duties on the products manufactured here and then compensating the manufacturer by an equal reduction on his raw material. The advantage of this can be easily seen; it enabled the government to go to the public and say, "Well, you have nothing to complain about; we reduced the duties on what you have to buy" and then they went back to the manufacturer and said, "Well, we did not hurt you any." The truth of this statement is very well borne out by the campaign speeches of some of the ministers. I know of nothing which so exemplifies the dextrous opportunism of the government so well as a poem written by Stephen Rudansky, a poet of the Ukraine, entitled, "We Need Friends Everywhere." The poem is as follows:
There was an old woman to church inclined, A church-going dame was she;
She brought some candles she opined Would be a mark of piety.
Wherever an icon she espied
She placed a candle to burn; _
"Two still remain, oh where", she cried,
"Shall I place each one in turn."
She spied St. Michael large and grand,
And Satan's image, both well done;
She placed two candles on a stand,
Near Michael and the Evil One.
The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich

The people stared, their rage waxed hot, "Old woman, stop," cried they;
"Oh fie on thee, oh knowst thou not,
"What waits thee on thy judgment day?"
"What sacrilege," the people cried,
"To place a candle there,
"To honor Satan, ah," they sighed,
"Twere better that the stand were hare."
The woman turned upon the crowd, Undaunted, bold was she;
"Speak not, oh people, out so loud "On matters of eternity."
For when you die you know not where Your spirit Shall reside;
"So why not see ere you get there,
"To you, no ill betide."
"It may be hell or paradise,
"The place which you will share So don't you think it very wise To make friends everywhere."
Do not the budgets of 1927, 1928 and 1929 well illustrate the propensities of the government for making friends everywhere, and do they not show the Minister of Finance lighting one candle to the farmer and worker and another to the magnate and industrialist, and are not those budgets evidences of how the present government try to satisfy the industrial east while at the same time appeasing the agricultural west with the result that we get a stand-pat budget which leaves the tariff strictly alone? The budget of 1927 was a stand-pat budget; so was that of 1928, and the budget of 1929 differs from those only in the fact it does not make any reduction in the income tax.
I have spoken of alibis and how the government have been able to fall back on these alibis when necessity dictated. In 1927 the alibi was the tariff board, and this year it is Hoover and the United States. The threat that the United States may raise a tariff wall against Canada has apparently saved the face of the government, for in a way it appears to lend a certain amount of justification to a remark made by the Minister of Finance, as follows:
The board is continuing its inquiries on which substantial progress has already been made into_ several larger problems which involve the consideration of whole tariff schedules, and the interrelation of many important Canadian industries. While those inquiries are being pursued opportunity will be afforded for consider-mg the possible effect on trade of changes being proposed in the tariff schedules of other countries, should they be implemented by legislation.
In other words, what the minister means is that we will not do anything with the tariff until we know what the United States intend doing. It not only helps the minister 
extricate himself from a very delicate situation, but it is drafted with a view to exonerate the tariff board from any charges which might be made against that seemingly useless body, which, after two years of effort and an expenditure of about $250,000, has absolutely no concrete achievement to its credit.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada are tired of alibis; the farmers of the west especially are tired of playing the part of a poor relation, as it were, thankful for the crumbs falling from the master's table, for all that is given to them by this budget is a few crumbs. It has long been my impression that reason has very little sway in the realm of politics under the party system. I have a suspicion that politics is run on the principle which Bamum enunciated many years ago. Force is the only thing that counts, and that force was very well exemplified in the budgets of 1927, 1928 and 1929. I think it is time that we snapped out of this state of affairs where idealism is recognized as being worse than useless and where force is the only thing that counts. I do not think the town has any right to lord it over the country, and I do not believe the people of the country should try to lord it over the town, but at the present time it seems to me that the town has the best of it. We do not come down here to destroy the factories of the electors who sent the members to the left of the Speaker to this parliament; all we ask is equal rights to all and special privileges to none. The situation appears to me to be somewhat similar to a pyramid standing on its apex; it is a mighty shaky affair. Until we can get a saner balance between the rural and urban interests we will continue to be like that pyramid and this country will be a mighty shaky affair, and this might be exemplified at the next election.
Members of the Liberal party may individually plead discipline and expediency, but that does not exonerate them from dereliction in the matter. I know how they pledged themselves to what would fit in with their party program, and I know something of the promises they made in preelection campaigns and the subsequent ridiculous excuses they had to make for the nonperformance of those pledges. Let us try to imagine the paradoxical position an honest member would be in on that side of the house. Let us imagine that that side of the house is an order called the order of the orange, the exalted ruler of which is the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). The emblem of this order is an orange placed on a receptacle before the exalted ruler. Suppose an honest member

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
like the member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) is brought in for initiation. In the course of that initiation he is asked to repeat these words, "I swear to abide by the rules of this order and accept the orange as an emblem thereof." But the member for Dauphin replies, "That is not an orange, it is a lemon." "The lord high executioner says it is an orange," retorts the hon. member for Marquette, with a wicked leer in his eye, "and so an orange it must be." "Well, all right" mumbles the member for Dauphin dejectedly, "if the executioner says it is an orange I will have to accept it as an orange but it looks for all the world like a lemon to me." And so if we apply the analogy to the realm of politics it seems to be a ridiculous statement to make to call the Liberal party a low tariff party when it is not a low tariff party; in other words, they have promised us oranges but gave us lemons instead. I have always considered the Liberal pronouncements on the budget as giving rise to but one remarkable thing, namely, the paradox wherein that party deceives itself to its own benefit at the expense of the public.
I was rather struck with the statement which the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) made last year when I was speaking on the budget. I made the remark that all the farmer members coming from the west should stick to the principle of low tariff; that we must either hang together on that tenet or hang separately when they got back home. I think it was the Minister of Immigration who interjected the remark, "Hear, hear". I wonder if he will make the same remark to-night.

speechtext:
If the minister
would make that remark then I would advise the Liberal-iProgressives sitting on that side of the house to hail the minister with these words, "We who are about to die salute thee."
I was rather struck with the statement that the government would refuse to support any extravagance in the spending of the taxpayers' money; I imagine they meant the spending of money for good roads and technical education. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that a good deal of money could be lapped off the grants to the Quebec hatbour, Ellis bay and other ventures and applied to the building of a much needed all-Canadian highway and technical schools. We would be doing much more good if we spent the money in that manner. In view
of the wonderful progress made by Germany and the United States in these matters, the large sums of money spent by those countries and the great international prestige gained thereby, I do mot agree with the minister that money spent on these enterprises is extravagance. The chief aim of anv government is the greatest happiness for the greatest number, and money spent on technical education which will ensure employment to a great number of our boys' and girls and keep them in the country is not extravagance; it is providence. I was rather impressed by the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) with regard to technical education. He said that research and technical education were entirely different things having nothing in common'. He said that it was only the aristocracy who could dabble in research. I agree with him in that regard, that it is only the university graduate who can take up that line of work. Technical education is limited to the young boys and girls of this country who have not had the opportunity of obtaining a university education. 1 have always considered too many of those coming out of our high schools were square pegs in round holes. I have always thought there was something wrong with our educational system. But technical education is a great thing for a country like Canada which has a Wonderful industrial future before it. I would rather be the Napoleon of bootblacks than a jack-of-all trades; I would rather be proficient in one thing than partly proficient in a hundred things, because I believe that if I were the Napoleon of bootblacks the wlorld would make a beaten path to my door and I would thereby be benefiting the country in which I lived, and also the country would benefit by me.
I will now pass to another matter of very great interest to the people of Canada, that of railroad building. There was a time when the leaders in all walks of life in Canada thought we were at least a half century ahead of our time in railway construction; that in view of our sparse papulation and limited productive capacity it was suicidal for our railways to make such heavy commitments with no other guarantee than an anticipation of a large business in the near future. Today we scout such timidity, activated as it was by the belief that railway construction was being overdone. On the contrary we believe that there is not enough of it, especially in such countries as that great hinterland which we call the Peace riven I believe that railways should precede popu-

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
lation. If we had a railway in the Peace river that would give the people in that country an outlet, it would be but a short time before that whole country would be very largely populated. We required railways very badly fifty years ago and we require them just as badly to-day, and therefore I am heartily in support of the extension branch line programs of both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. I am, however, more deeply interested i* the Canadian National Railways, because it is a publicly-owned railway in which the people are deeply concerned, and in which they have a great financial interest. At the same time, however, I do not wish to deprive the Canadian Pacific Railway of its just share of railway building. I believe there is plenty of room for both railways, but I am also of the view that we should put both of those railways on an equal footing. I am very sorry that the resolution proposed by the bon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) got such little support in the railway committee the other day. I think if his resolution had passed i't would have solved one of our great railway problems in Canada to-day, that of putting both railways on an equal footing.
As I review the railway situation in Canada, both railways have been pioneers in certain parts of the Dominion, especially in the west. The Canadian National Railways has been the pioneer in the northern part of Canada, therefore we believe that they have certain prior rights to large areas in the northern part of Canada. The Canadian Pacific Railway has been the pioneer in the southern part of Alberta, and the southern part of Canada, and it is the opinion of some people that they have prior rights because of the pioneering work done by them in that part of the Dominion. But the situation is becoming more complicated now because both railways desire to build in the northern part of Canada. I believe that- some agreement should be reached by which we can allocate the territory that has to foe served by proposed new branches of both companies in northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta. And unless we make this agreement the situation will become very complicated indeed. If 'hon. members will remember the Willingdon-Edmonton situation of last year, and the rank parallelism and high-handed competitive poaching caused thereby, they will, I am sure, before any charters are granted to private companies subject the applications therefor to the closest and most exacting scrutiny. The Toronto Telegram has sized up the situation in an editorial which reads as follows:

If public ownership of railways is not to die in Canada the national railways must be put on an equal footing with the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to franchises. As things stand at present the privately-owned system is at an immense advantage. It goes to parliament and gets a job lot of franchises. The routes they cover may or may not be built in the five years the franchises cover. If the branches are not built, it is possible, even probable, that the franchises will be renewed.
The Canadian National Railways on the other hand, must come to parliament with a three-year program for which the money must be voted. Also the work must be completed within the three years. i	_	_
The advantage the Canadian Pacific Railway has is that it can preempt territory and build only if development justifies it. In other words, the Canadian Pacific Railway can option territory without paying out a dollar. It can also, and at the same price, head off extensions that the Canadian National Railways are not ready to go on with at the present time. Baldly, the Canadian Pacific Railway is in a position to hedge around the Canadian National Railways with franchises that threaten its entire future.
Fair play demands that the railways be put on an equal footing. The Canadian Pacific Railway, when granted a franchise, should be required to give an undertaking that the line will be built within three years. And this undertaking should be ironclad.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Pacific has a great advantage over the Canadian National, as has been exemplified in the construction of the Willingdon-Edmonton line, and if we are not careful the same thing will be experienced in other parts of Canada. I think that the only thing to do in order to eradicate a condition of this kind is to put both lines on an equal footing.
Now, what is this Willingdon-Edmonton situation to which I have just referred? In the year 1927 the Canadian Pacific railway was granted a charter to complete the line from Cutknife to Whitford lake. The construction was completed in 1928. During the summer and fall of 1928 they continued construction and finished the line to Edmonton. But before the line had been completed to Edmonton a dispute arose between the two companies, which culminated in a hearing before the Board of Railway Commissioners in Edmonton on June 14, 1928. The Canadian National Railways protested against allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to build their branch line from Willingdon to Edmonton, on the ground that they had no charter rights thereto. In reply, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company stated the Willingdon-Edmonton line could be built under the authority granted for the construction of the Swift Current Northwesterly branch, the route may of which was approved in June, 1919. I might point out here, Mr. Speaker, that only

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
a few small pieces of the grade between Swift Current and Willingdon have been completed, and at that very far apart.
The Swift Current northwesterly branch was built from Swift Current to Empress, about 112 miles, between 1911 and 1914, and a further section between Coronation and Lorraine, about 20 miles, between 1914 and 1915. In 1919 they again took up the question of the extension of this line to Edmonton, and secured the approval of the then Minister of Railways and Canals for a revision of the route, abandoning about fifty miles of the 310 miles already approved to Chatton and extending it via Whitford lake to Edmonton. At the session of parliament in the same year the company obtained authority to extend its Cutknife line to a point in the vicinity of Whitford lake where it was to join the Swift Current-Edmonton line.
In their evidence before the Board of Railway Commissioners the Canadian Pacific Railway Company argued that they were acting' under their main charter granted in 1881, by which they were given power to build branches from their main line to any part in Canada. The Canadian National Railway Company claimed that branch lines had to be built continuously from the main line, and that in this case-Willingdon-Edmonton-it was a mere eighty-mile isolated chunk having no real connection with the main line. As a counter argument the Canadian Pacific Railway Company claimed that they could begin building any branch line from whichever end they chose, they could build isolated chunks no matter how far separated, so long as the plan had been approved by the Dominion railway board. "For example," said Mr. Ruel, vicepresident of the Canadian National Railways legal department, "the Canadian Pacific Railway by their interpretation might build a railway from Port Nelson on the Hudson bay across the northwestern part of Canada to the mouth of the Mackenzie river, and say it was really a branch from the main line, since the whole plan included a line from Port Nelson down to the main line someday." It would appear, Mr. Speaker, that when we allowed the Canadian Pacific Railway to build across Canada in 1881, we gave that company a charter with very wide powers, powers that were bound to bring both companies into open warfare sooner or later. It is essential therefore that parliament should find some way of putting these two systems on an equality with respect to charter rights. Allow me to read what the Free Press has to say on this point:-
The west has already had examples of Canadian National Railways being blocked in what it regarded as its own territory when the senate rejected its claims on the ground that the Canadian Pacific Railway had obtained a previous charter which it had not executed, the Canadian Pacific Railway was merely reserving the territory for a period of years until it was ready to go in. If allowed to proceed on the five-year charter basis as against the fact that the Canadian National Railways, before it will be granted a charter, must obtain the approval of parliament for the money to build the projected line, the private company can cut the ground from under the government system. The private company can obtain charters for any part of the country where it might have an idea a mineral strike might be made, a power site developed, or a pulp mill constructed. The Canadian National Railways is prevented from doing anything of the kind. It is obvious that parliament must work out some system that will put the two systems on an equality with respect to charter rights. The simple plan would be to follow the procedure now applied to the Canadian National. When the Canadian Pacific Railway sought a charter it would have to bring before parliament the authorization of its shareholders to spend the money on the proposed road within a three-year period, and forfeit its claim to the territory at the end of three years if the line had not been built.
Such a system would give reality to the business of chartering railway lines. It would be fairer to every one. If it is a good system for the government railway system, it should be a good system for the private company.
My objection to the Willingdon-Edmonton line was that it did not go further north; that it paralleled and duplicated the Canadian National railway for forty miles, thus destroying the business chances of such towns as Lamont, Bruederheim and Fort Saskatchewan, in close proximity to which other small stations have been built along the new Canadian Pacific Railway branch. I was very glad to see the railway built in that part of the country, because the farmers had lived there for thirty years, many of them having a haul of thirty-five or forty-five miles to the nearest station and they very much needed railway facilities. But I was very much against the Canadian Pacific Railway building their line in such close proximity to the Canadian National. For forty miles the present Canadian Pacific parallels the Canadian National, and it is one of the most glaring cases of competitive poaching that I know of. Unless this house does something to eradicate this condition of affairs in Canada, we might some day in other parts of the country have situations of the same character. Therefore I think it is high time for parliament to do something with respect to this railway situation, and the best thing we can do is to put the two railways on an equal footing.
The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCLAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up at any length the time of the house, for, if I mistake not, it is the desire of hon. members on both sides that the business of the house be expedited, consistently, however, with due consideration of all questions which may be submitted.
It is unquestionably a fact that the presentation of the budget is the outstanding event at every session of parliament. It is always most anxiously awaited not only by the house, but by every constituency throughout Canada. We have not been disappointed in our anticipations. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has again not only demonstrated his keen executive foresight in matters pertaining to the successful administration of the affairs of our country, but has also clearly pointed out the enormous development which has taken place in Canada during the last six years, particularly during the year ending 1928, and has most conclusively given proof to all the countries with which we do business, in other words to the world at large, of the solid foundation upon which rests the financial structure of our country.
The unprecedented prosperity throughout Canada is attributable above all to a kind Providence, and as well to the indefatigable and persistent efforts of our Canadian people, coupled with the stimulating effects of a government whose sane economic policy and fostering influences have contributed so mucii to the success of every branch of industry.
We marvel, Mr. Speaker, when looking back over the years, at the enormous expansion of our external trade since 1922, which has within the last eleven months reached the stupendous figure of 82,401,627,966, brought about by the opening up of every possible avenue of trade, by the t negotiation of trade treaties with all the important countries of the world, and by the granting of a ten per cent preference to all imports from British possessions entering Canada through Canadian ports. This ten per cent preference has greatly stimulated business in the ports of St. John and Halifax and ports along the St. Lawrence, but I regret that the shipping interests of the states of Maine and Massachusetts were a little annoyed at our policy in that regard. It was, however, just another successful business adventure by the government to stimulate and increase trade through our ports, and not, by any means, a retaliatory measure. We desire to live on the most mutual good fellowship terms with our American friends, who, I am sure, are conscious of the fact that we are endeavouring in our own way, as they are in theirs,

to increase the happiness of our people. This enormous expansion has had most beneficial results; it has enabled the Minister of Finance each year since 1922 to proclaim surpluses instead of deficits, aggregating in the last six years the grand total of $226,780,000, and resulting in a decrease of interest charges to the extent of the tidy sum of $16,340,013. Not only this, but by the application of a sane, moderate customs tariff policy and the reduction of the sales tax, stamp tax, and various other forms of taxation, we are pleased to note that the government has been able to save to the people of Canada the large sum of $241,000,000. Surely this is a showing of which we should be justly proud, and for which, on behalf of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent, I desire to extend commendations to the Minister of Finance.
Now, sir, in so far as conditions in New Brunswick are concerned, I may say that agriculture, which is our basic industry, was not during the last year as prosperous as we would have desired, due to a depressed state of the potato market, resulting not from any fault of the government, as some would have us believe-for we in New Brunswick are fully convinced that the prosperity of a country is dependent above all things upon the industry and efforts of its people in every sphere of activity-but due to a super abundant crop throughout Canada and particularly in the United States, where notwithstanding the almost prohibitive duty of fifty cents per hundred pounds we have been able, including what we have placed on the Cuban market, to dispose of the major part of our surplus production of potatoes. But if the extreme views of the protectionists in the United States prevail with respect to an increase in the tariff on agricultural products, it will be our duty to look to the east, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) very properly stated in an address made while on a visit to the maritime provinces some two years ago, making reference to the West Indies trade agreement. I sincerely regret the apparent attitude of the extreme protectionists of the United States, for if carried into effect it will no doubt materially affect our exports. However, I am still hopeful, and as an example of the sentiment which prevails among the more cautious, may I be permitted to quote an editorial published in the Atlanta Journal as appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of March 12, 1928:
There are those among the protectionists themselves who realize that America's interest in Canada is such as to render very dubious the adoption of a policy which would discourage trade relations between the countries, and

thus arouse antagonism that might prove far more costly to America than any passing advantage from higher duties on our Canadian imports. Canada can no longer be regarded as merely a foreign country and treated as such by the United States. These countries have too much in common and there now exists if not by treaty, yet by custom and practice, an interdependence that cannot be ignored. American investments in Canada to-day amount to billions of dollars, and not even Britain as a whole has contributed so largely to Canadian development as has America.
The Atlanta Journal concludes:
It is needless to remark that American capital in Canada is subject to the laws and customs of the Dominion and dependent thereon for fair treatment and protection. Small wonder when we consider this situation, that there is disquietude in the citadel of some of our protectionists when -the tariff makers at Washington threaten excessive and prohibitive rates on Canadian imports. American business well may be aware.
This, Mr. Speaker, is very significant and a very timely warning.
Coming to the question of our fisheries, I may say that the year 1928 has been a fairly successful one. It would have been more successful had not the price of live lobsters ___which has become a very important industry along the counties of Kent and Westmorland-on the United States market fallen from 25 cents a pound in 1927 to 15 and 16 cents in 1928. With a corresponding drop for lobsters sold by the fishermen to the .canning industries, this very materially affected the receipts from that source, but the loss iwas offset to some extent by the catch of oysters, particularly in the bays of Buctouche and Cocagne in my constituency. Only about
1.000	barrels were taken in 1927, as against
3.000	barrels more than in 1928. This increase is due to nothing more or less than the strict enforcement of the fishery regulations. It is indeed a very profitable source of revenue to those living in the immediate vicinity, during the legal fishing season, from the 25th of September until the ice forms about the 1st of December. The epicure who desires an excellent barrel of oysters I would advise to ask for the famous Buctouche aind Cocagne bay oysters.
Thanks to the government's initiative, we now have a fortnightly service of five steamers plying between the Atlantic ports of St. John and Halifax and the British West Indies, luxuriously and comfortably equipped for the business and tourist trade, which is bound to develop. These steamers are also provided with cold storage and all the necessary facilities for the transportation of all classes of merchandise. There is no question about the developing of a large trade within a very
few years with the British West Indies, whose population and that of the American republics total about fifteen millions. There is undoubtedly a vast trading opportunity in that direction. It now only lies with the business men and manufacturers of Canada, and particularly of the maritimes, coupled with the assistance of our trade commissioners, to get busy and go after the trade.
Now, sir, coming to the industrial situation, in New Brunswick, I may say that we anticipate a large development of the pulp and paper industry in the near future at Dalhousie and Athol in the county of Restigouche, and near Chatham in the county of Northumberland. And I have no hesitancy in saying that this development is wholly due to the determination and vision of the Foster and Veniot administration of provincial affairs in the inauguration of a public ownership hydro policy. Had that policy been continued instead of bartering away the Grand falls hydro power site to three private pulp and paper corporations, we would in the course of a few years be distributing power not only to these pulp and paper industries, but also to other industries in various parts of the province. Then the whole population in course of time could enjoy a prosperity such as has been realized in the province of Ontario under a policy of public ownership. But, Mr. Speaker, time. I hope, will bring about a realization of the aspirations -of the people of New Brunswick in that regard.
Coming to the matter of expenditures on breakwaters, the construction and repairs to wharves in the interest of the successful prosecution of the fisheries by our fishermen, as well as in the interest of shipping along the eastern coast of New Brunswick, I must say that there is no justification for the insinuations of extravagance made by some hon. members on the other side of th-e house because of the necessity of the government in seeing to the requirements of New Brunswick and of the maritimes as a whole in this regard. I -can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that when a request is -made and favourably reported upon after investigation by the engineering branch at St. John, the work a-sked for is absolutely necessary, because a staff of engineers more competent and -more devoted to the safeguarding -of the people's money, -ait the head of whom is Mr. Ge-offrey Stead in the capacity of district engineer for the province of New Brunswick, cannot be found in any part of Canada.
In conclusion I desire to thank th-e government for what it has done in this matter of public works in my constituency, and for the
